caseName: Palm Beach Florida Hotel & Office Building Corp. v. Nantucket Enterprises, Inc.
court: Florida Fourth District Court of Appeal
keyFacts: Nantucket Enterprises leased restaurant, lounge, kitchen, atrium, gazebo, ballroom, and boardroom space (roughly 20,281 sq. ft.) inside an Embassy Suites hotel. After a permitting/renovation dispute led the city to deem the restaurant unsafe, the landlord locked the tenant out and terminated the lease without going through the courts, even though the lease itself contained a self-help clause.
outcome: Directed verdict for the tenant on wrongful eviction affirmed on appeal; the appellate court held that Florida Statutes section 83.20 requires a landlord to recover possession only by court order, tenant surrender, or tenant abandonment, and a lease's private self-help clause cannot override that statutory requirement. The $8.8 million damages award was affirmed.
dollarAmountBasis: Damages for wrongful eviction (lost business value/profits) as found by the trial court and affirmed on appeal
notes: Widely cited as the leading example of a large commercial wrongful-eviction verdict; landlord's contractual self-help clause was unenforceable because Florida statute requires judicial process regardless of lease terms.

keyFacts: Landlord Wiley leased a building to Berg to operate the Family Affair Restaurant. After a dispute over remodeling and health-code violations, Wiley changed the locks and excluded Berg while she was temporarily off the premises, without resorting to legal process.
outcome: Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed judgment for the tenant, holding that a landlord may no longer use self-help/forcible re-entry against a tenant in possession, even a holdover tenant, and must use judicial process. This case abolished self-help eviction for commercial landlords in Minnesota.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury award of $31,000 for lost profits plus $3,540 for loss of chattels resulting from the wrongful lockout
notes: Landmark case establishing Minnesota's flat prohibition on commercial self-help eviction; frequently cited nationwide in property-law casebooks.

keyFacts: Commercial tenants defaulted on rent. The landlord, without notice, retook possession and rerented the premises pursuant to a lease clause allowing self-help reentry, then sued the tenants for accruing rent; the tenants counterclaimed for trespass and breach of quiet enjoyment.
outcome: Trial court's summary judgment for the landlord affirmed. The Georgia Court of Appeals held that where a commercial lease grants the landlord a right to reenter and retake possession without judicial process, the landlord may lawfully do so if it can be accomplished without a breach of the peace.
notes: Principle-only case (landlord prevailed). Illustrates Georgia's conditional allowance of commercial self-help eviction when the lease authorizes it and no breach of peace occurs — useful as a contrast to prohibited-self-help states.

keyFacts: A tenant leasing office space fell behind on rent; after warning him in writing that failure to pay could result in the premises being locked, the landlords removed his remaining office furniture, equipment, and law books to storage when he did not pay.
outcome: Judgment for the landlord affirmed; the court found the lockout and removal of chattels to be a lawful, peaceable self-help repossession under the circumstances, not an unlawful conversion.
notes: Principle-only case (landlord prevailed) illustrating that peaceable self-help with prior notice can defeat a commercial tenant's conversion claim in a state that permits conditional self-help.

keyFacts: A landlord locked out a tenant who was reportedly behind on rent, changing the locks and posting an eviction notice without following Tennessee's judicial eviction process, then retained the tenant's personal property left inside.
outcome: Court of Appeals affirmed the landlord's liability for conversion, holding that locking the tenant out while retaining the tenant's property inside constituted conversion. It vacated a $5,000 punitive-damages award for lack of specific findings and remanded for the trial court to recalculate.
dollarAmountBasis: Conversion damages measured by the present-day value of the retained personal property (amount not stated in secondary source); $5,000 punitive damages award vacated and remanded for proper findings
notes: Good illustration of the conversion theory layered onto a wrongful-lockout claim, and of appellate scrutiny of punitive-damages findings in this context.

caseName: Eun Bok Lee v. Ho Chang Lee
court: Court of Appeals of Texas, First District (Houston)
keyFacts: A landlord locked out a commercial tenant who had operated a gas station for over a decade, in the midst of a dispute over ownership of underground fuel storage tanks. The landlord changed the locks without posting the written notice required by Texas Property Code section 93.002(f) (name/contact info for obtaining the new key).
outcome: Court of appeals affirmed judgment largely for the tenant on the wrongful-eviction/Property Code 93.002 claim, but reversed a treble-damages award tied to the security deposit because that theory was not properly pleaded or tried by consent. Tenant also recovered on unrelated unjust-enrichment and overcharged-rent claims.
dollarAmountBasis: Statutory wrongful-eviction actual damages ($5,000) plus related rent damages ($2,375) under Tex. Prop. Code § 93.002; excludes ~$145,000 in unrelated unjust-enrichment, security-deposit, and overcharged-rent recoveries and interest/fees in the same suit
notes: Rare case actually applying Chapter 93's specific notice requirement (93.002(f)) rather than just citing the statute generally. Total judgment in the case (~$152,000) mixes lockout damages with unrelated claims, so only the wrongful-eviction component is reported as dollarAmount.

court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Third Circuit
keyFacts: Platinum City leased space in Lake Charles for a nightclub at $4,000/month. After a rent check bounced and Platinum City fell two months behind, the landlord sent a five-day notice to vacate; when the tenant ignored it and kept operating, the landlord changed the locks rather than filing an eviction suit.
outcome: The Third Circuit held the landlord's self-help lockout was a wrongful eviction under Louisiana law (which requires judicial process, absent abandonment), but found the tenant failed to prove its claimed lost-equipment and lost-profits damages. The court also reduced the landlord's attorney-fee award from $12,725 to $1,750 because most fees stemmed from defending the improper eviction rather than collecting rent.
dollarAmountBasis: Tenant's wrongful-eviction damages claim was rejected for lack of proof; only the landlord's reduced attorney-fee recovery ($1,750, down from $12,725) is a documented dollar figure
notes: Citation (81 So. 3d 780) obtained via secondary legal-search corroboration rather than direct retrieval of the court's slip opinion; facts and outcome corroborated by a law-firm case summary. Useful cautionary example: establishing liability for wrongful lockout is not the same as proving damages.

court: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina
keyFacts: Franchisees operating a Family Fare gas station/convenience store in Winston-Salem were confronted by a company representative who entered the store, confiscated the safe key, took over the cash register, and had a locksmith change the locks after the franchisor terminated the franchise and lease agreements, without obtaining a court order.
outcome: On summary judgment, the district court denied the defendants' motion as to the plaintiffs' North Carolina wrongful-eviction and unfair-and-deceptive-trade-practices (N.C.G.S. § 75-1.1) claims, holding that a forcible self-help commercial eviction can violate North Carolina's public policy against self-help and can separately support a UDTPA claim (which carries treble damages and fee-shifting). The wrongful-eviction/UDTPA claims proceeded past summary judgment; a specific damages figure for these claims was not identified in available secondary sources.
notes: Principle-only entry: confirms that forcible commercial self-help lockouts can independently trigger North Carolina's UDTPA treble-damages/fee-shifting statute, not just an ordinary wrongful-eviction claim. Final jury verdict amount (if any; case may have settled) was not located and is not reported here.

caseName: Emma Green Rest. LLC v. Blackridge Dev. Corp.
court: Supreme Court of New York, Westchester County
keyFacts: A restaurant operator ("Amelia's Kitchen") leased commercial space from Blackridge. The landlord could not produce evidence of a lawful eviction or 72-hour statutory notice before the tenant was excluded from the premises and lost possession.
outcome: Following a non-jury trial, the court found the tenant was unlawfully locked out without proper notice or due process, granted rent abatement for November 2018 through July 2019, and held the tenant entitled to recover actual and compensatory damages (including attorney's fees, costs, and disbursements) in an amount to be determined in further proceedings.
dollarAmountBasis: Court found landlord liable and awarded rent abatement plus a right to actual/compensatory damages, attorney's fees, costs and disbursements, but the specific dollar figure was left to be determined and was not located in available secondary sources
notes: Decision establishes liability for an illegal commercial lockout under New York law but the case summary available does not report a final damages figure.

court: Arizona Court of Appeals, Division Two
keyFacts: The Janeses leased space in the El Capri Shopping Center for a women's clothing store under a five-year lease beginning September 1975. After falling behind on rent for December 1975 and January 1976, the landlord (Chesin/Country Escrow Service) excluded them from the premises. This was the second appeal in the case, after an earlier remand for a new trial on breach of contract and conversion (Country Escrow Service v. Janes, 121 Ariz. 511, 591 P.2d 999 (App. 1979)).
outcome: On retrial, the jury found for the tenants on their conversion claim (the breach-of-contract count having been dismissed) and awarded substantial compensatory and punitive damages; the appellate court's judgment addressed post-trial issues from that verdict.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury verdict of $7,741.29 compensatory damages plus $110,000 punitive damages for conversion arising from the commercial lockout
notes: One of the larger punitive-damages awards found for a commercial lockout/conversion claim; illustrates that egregious conduct during a lockout (not just the exclusion itself) can support outsized punitive damages even in a state that otherwise recognizes some rights of self-help.
